newsitem.title: POLAND: Thousands of Czechs, Poles brace for surging flood.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Czechs, Poles brace for surging flood.

text.p: Floods in the Czech Republic and south Poland had claimed 55 lives by Friday and thousands of people waited fearfully in the path of the raging waters.
As high water advanced down rivers towards communities hastily preparing flood defences, both governments mustered funds to help victims rebuild shattered homes and lives.

"There are 365,000 hectares, or about 3,500 sq km (2,170 sq miles) under water," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told public radio in Poland, where 50 towns and 280 villages have already been hit by floods often reaching rooftops.

Although sun returned to the skies over southern Poland and waters receded in some areas, a swell swept north along the Odra river. Having swamped parts of Opole city, it bore down on the major centre Wroclaw.
Emergency services sent sappers to blow up dykes south of Wroclaw to disperse excess water into the countryside before it hit the city, Private Radio Zet reported from the scene.
But in the village of Lany desperate farmers drove away the engineers with threats and removed the explosives, it said.
In the Czech Republic the worst floods this century, reported to have claimed at least 32 lives, began moving south and almost one-third of the country was still in danger.
Troops and firemen were evacuating residents on Friday from towns and villages downstream on the Morava and Opava rivers.

Anxious to avoid delay in rebuilding, the Czech parliament approved government requests on Friday to approve the issue of up to five billion crowns ($150 million) of bonds to fund emergency relief, and also released five billion in privatisation proceeds.
The government earlier approved a package of about one billion crowns from various sources and pledged more than 12 billion, while President Vaclav Havel dug into his own pocket.
"Everything that can be done to help is important. This is a test for us all," said Havel, who overflew the hardest hit areas of Moravia on Thursday.
In Poland, where a national flood crisis committee spokesman said the death toll was 23, opposition critics accused the government of inadequate rescue and relief efforts.

The issue threatened to hurt the main ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), the party of former communists, facing a close fight against rightists grouped round the Solidarity trade union in parliamentary elections on September 21.
"The state has shown itself totally helpless and weak," a Solidarity chief, Maciej Jankowski, told a news conference.
Premier Cimoszewicz argued that while in some areas rescue efforts had fallen down, overall they had been adequate given the unprecedented and unpredictable disaster.
"Unfortunately many people are playing politics in these circumstances," said Cimoszewicz.

Poland's government on Thursday decided to squeeze 500 million zlotys ($155 million) from budget reserves to help a long-term recovery plan now being drafted to help rebuild flood-hit homes, roads and 160 damaged bridges.

In both countries some major factories had to close or cut production, including Czech carmaker Skoda Automobilova a.s., while dealers said floods contributed to a slide in their currencies on foreign exchange markets.
Poland's farm ministry said it could not even begin to assess crop damage yet, but it had enough food reserves to avoid additional imports.
Rains from Saturday to Tuesday also gave Austria its worst flooding this century, costing billions of schillings.
Worst-hit were flood plains in Lower Austria where water touched the roofs of houses and several bridges were swept away, while hundreds of people were evacuated.

Much further east, the former Soviet republic of Azerbaijan appealed for help from the United Nations to tackle floods which have killed 11 people, destroyed or damaged more than 7,000 homes, wrecked roads and bridges and wiped out several thousand hectares of wheat and cotton crops.
Floods sent raw sewage flowing through dozens of towns and villages in central Azerbaijan, prompting fears of epidemics.
